title: The Reparations Decade: a UN Vote, Jamaica's Privy Council Case, Namibia's Talks | The Six, Ep. 19
lede: In March, 123 countries voted for a UN resolution calling the transatlantic slave trade the gravest crime against humanity; three voted against and 52 abstained. The African Union has declared a Decade of Justice for Africans, 2026 to 2035, and the first tests of the reparations claim are now in a London court and in talks between Namibia and Germany.
keyPoints: UN General Assembly, Mar. 25, 2026: 123 for, 3 against (the United States, Israel, Argentina), 52 abstentions including EU member states. The resolution, led by Ghana, is non-binding and calls for dialogue on apologies, restitution, compensation and rehabilitation (PassBlue; UN News).

In February the AU Assembly endorsed a 2026–2035 Decade of Justice for Africans, with Ghana's President John Mahama as champion, and noted that its reparations programme is underfunded (AU Assembly decision Dec.942).

The most cited cost estimate, by The Brattle Group in 2023, puts reparations for transatlantic slavery at $100–131 trillion: $77–108 trillion for harm during slavery and $23 trillion after it (The Brattle Group).

Jamaica petitioned King Charles on Sept. 7; the case is now with the Privy Council, Britain's case is due by Nov. 20 and a preliminary hearing is set for the week of Mar. 8, 2027 (Jamaica Information Service).

Germany offered Namibia €1.1 billion over 30 years in 2021 for the 1904–1908 genocide, framed as development aid; it was rejected, and Namibia's president wants a revised declaration concluded by end-2026 (The Namibian).
